utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you've made a Rule 70 application to us. There's a measure of urgency about it. Unless there was any dissent from counsel for the accused, then we would order responses to that by Wednesday. You've also made an application for additional protective measures for K79. When do you envisage that witness commencing testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we thought that this witness would go into tomorrow. Witness Vollebaek was scheduled to start Wednesday. He doesn't arrive until late Tuesday, I think. So, we might run short tomorrow and then K79 would follow Vollebaek probably starting on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again, we would order responses to that motion by I think Tuesday evening in that case, so that we can look at it first thing on Wednesday just in case it's necessary to advance that witness's testimony. Your next witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Our next witness will be K90, 9-0. Your Honour, this witness will testify as both viva voce and a 92 ter based on his written statement. We filed a supplemental information on Friday and indicated that we were going to make an oral motion at this time, Your Honour, to supplement the original 65 ter to lead evidence on some of that information provided in the supplemental information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I regret, I don't have this document, Mr. Hannis. All of this must have been happening very late on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So one's being printed just now. Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. While we're waiting on that, Your Honour, I can provide you with some additional information. This is a witness for whom protective measures of pseudonym, image, and voice distortion was granted. His evidence pertains to paragraphs 25 through 32, 72(H), and 75(H). And with regard to his written statement, Your Honour, paragraphs 3 through 23 talk about activities in Bosnia in 1992 through 1995. I don't intend to ask him any questions about that evidence. I only left it in the statement for the purposes of showing this witness's background in the military and as it pertains to any weight you might give his evidence about military procedures, uniforms, insignia, weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that it's -- the contents of paragraph 8 of this supplemental information sheet that you invite us to allow you to lead evidence on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was a follow-up to the paragraph in his statement where he said he had additional information about incidents in Kosovo that I mentioned last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there opposition to that? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any, and I don't know about my colleagues. I have no opposition to that. I do, however, have opposition to the suggestion that paragraphs 3 through I think it's 23 -- 3 through 23 should be left in the 65 ter statement. They're totally irrelevant to any issue in this case at all. They go way beyond providing background about his military career which could be elicited in, I would say, three minutes of direct examination. So I would ask that paragraphs 3 through 23 be stricken from the 65 ter statement -- I'm sorry, 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we agree with the submission that it would be unduly prejudicial to include paragraphs 3 to 23 so far as they relate to the events that took place. There would be a temptation to compare some of these, indeed, to events in Kosovo. On the other hand, we agree with Mr. Ackerman also that it is relevant to know the military experience of the witness and that there are references in there just to his experience in general, but, for example, there is also reference to paramilitaries; and to some extent, some of that evidence and how he recognised them and so on would be relevant. So we invite you to lead that as oral evidence, but we also order you to produce a statement that excludes paragraphs 3 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can have the witness. We need to go into closed session for the witness to come into court. And, of course, we will allow you to lead evidence from the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir. Good morning, sir. In the interests of security, you will be known to us as Witness K90. We will not be referring -- do you hear me now? In the interests of security, you will be referred to as Witness K90. We will not be referring to your name at any stage; that is no discourtesy. It is in your own personal interests. Would you now please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, what are the documents you are arranging there. Can you tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me, Mr. Hannis, with the document that the witness has --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From here, Your Honour, it looks like a copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We -- I think you should --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you made notes on this statement yourself, or is it a clear copy of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what you should do is just put that document aside. If anyone wishes you to look at your statement, a copy will be provided for you. Now, the first counsel this morning to ask you questions will be for the Prosecution, and that's Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I will begin, Witness K90, by showing you some documents, and we will deal with that first by handing you Exhibit P2631. Sir, this is a document containing personal information about your name and your date of birth. I want you to just look at it and read it to yourself and then tell us if that information is correct, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender that pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and may that be filed under seal as the ordinary process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I would like to hand you two documents. Exhibit P2391 is your statement to the ICTY dated December 2002 and P2640 is a redacted version of that where we have blacked out the personal identifying information about you. Could you look first at the unredacted version, P2391, and tell me if you recognise it as your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the one that you and I did not see during our preparation or proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have a chance to -- did you have a chance to review it and make some changes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand that comment, Mr. Hannis, "the one that you and I did not see." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, you said "the one you and I did not see." Are you referring to Exhibit 2640, the one that has the redactions on it, parts of it had been blacked out. Is that the one that you and I did not see at the time of the proofing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the unredacted one, the one that is completely clear, you said you made some changes during the proofing. I want to ask you about those now. At paragraph 28, you indicated that we should change the reference to the 542nd Armoured Mechanised Brigade to the 549th Motorised Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 39, there was a reference to a man who worked in the municipal building. You told us on Friday that that was not correct and should not be in there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to paragraph 41, you were talking about one of your unit's task being to tell people to move out, but you wanted to add it was not your unit's primary task to do that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 43, it originally read that you did this in most of the villages around Djakovica. You told us that should be changed to read "some of the villages."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 52, where you were talking about seeing scores of displaced Albanian civilians walking past your command post, you indicated that that number was more than 500.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, numbers are a relative thing. Now it's a question of bidding. Was it 300? Was it 500? There were a lot of people. The number can be 300; it can be 500. I cannot say with certainty whether it was 300 or 500, but the fact remains that there were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Should we correct that then, because currently we said it should be changed to more than 500. Are you not comfortable with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Let it be around 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'll make a note of that. Now -- and then you told us about some additional incidents that we'll talk about later. But with regard to those changes we've just talked about, having noted those, can you attest now to the Judges that your written statement accurately reflects your declaration or your evidence and it is what you would say today if you were asked those questions again, the same questions about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, let me just find this. There are some imprecisions in this statement; and as we looked at that, we corrected some of them. Let me just find this concerning the relocation of people or the number of persons who got killed at the site and a few other things that you and I discussed on Friday. That is to say, let me just find this. Was it paragraph 41? I think it was. Yes. Paragraph 41 through 45. There are some imprecisions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to tell us what those are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: For example, my unit had the task to order the Albanian villagers to leave their homes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we -- may I intercede at this point. I had a concern regarding identity and naming his direct superiors may lead to his identification. I would like to go into private session and redact that portion where we mention a couple of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that course of action? Very well, we shall do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry I interrupted before. You were telling us about your unit had the task to order villagers to leave their homes, and I think you were saying this was ordered by your commander. What did you want to explain that you say is an imprecision in your statement in paragraphs 41 through 45 about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: On Friday I said to you, and today I'm going to say to this honourable Trial Chamber, that what is written here is not quite precise; that is to say, that my major never ordered the expulsion of villagers, that is to say, to have them expelled to Albania. The order was always that these people should be directed towards Djakovica and the first villages near Djakovica. For what reason? I cannot go into that. Now, further on, if later on, we, the soldiers on that territory, allow them to go back to their homes and take their personal belongings for themselves and their families, that is, that is not expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, yes. Yes. The population was not relocated until the cluster bombs started falling. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, around mid-April, roughly, 1999. No. I cannot recall the exact date, but from mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anything else you wanted to correct or clarify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Not in this part. But when you start examining me, then if I have something to raise I will, yes, so that we wouldn't read out the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. With those clarifications noted, now are you satisfied that your written statement accurately reflects your declaration and is the answers that you would give if asked about those same matters today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, with small corrections, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you think of any other small corrections you want to bring to our attention now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Just a second, please. Just a second, please. Yes. Yes, paragraph 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I returned to the major and reported what I had seen. He started to swear and was very angry because this was happening. I personally saw at least four groups of men being taken to the compound, and they number from five to over ten men. What is correct is that only the last group had between eight and ten men. It would be one, two, three, so you cannot say exactly that every group numbered ten men. There were smaller groups, and the last one numbered eight to ten men; that is to say, that the last group had eight to ten men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Not for the time being; but if there is anything, I will say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of that, perhaps I'll move to tender his statement at the end when I've identified whether there are any additional clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, you tell us in your statement that you initially did your mandatory national service in 1980. At that time what was your military job? Were you an infantry man or what did you do in 1980?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I was in the border unit, infantry, in fact, infantry. The border control unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we read in your statement that you volunteered for the army and you fought in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You tell us at that time you didn't receive any training about the Geneva Convention and Rules of War. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that you later, in May 1992, became a professional soldier and part of a military police unit. Did you have any training about the Geneva Convention and Rules of War at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, can you explain the difference for me between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judge what you mean by "absolutely."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: This means that we received training on all international conventions relating to Law of War. This was a serious unit, and it was the kind of unit where you couldn't be without undergoing such training.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That leads me to my next question. Can you explain the difference between a volunteer, which you were in Croatia, and a professional soldier, that you were after May 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, there's no comparing the two. I cannot draw any comparisons because the latter was a professional unit where you had the chain of command, the system of issuing orders, subordination was in place; whereas, the former was something completely different. It was also a part of the former Yugoslav military, but there were no officers, no commanding officers, in the field. You had reservists, just as we were. They were in command of those units and that's just not the same. It cannot be the same. There was no discipline, not to the extent that existed in the unit where I served as a professional soldier. So for all intents and purposes, no comparison can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were in a volunteer unit, to who -- not a name, but what rank did your commander have, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I think he was a colonel, but I only saw him twice. I don't think that I would be able to recognise him at all. I don't think that he ever came to this area where we were. He had his command post, and he never left it, at least I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any major or captain or lieutenant who was in the field with your unit that was commanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I think there was a captain, but I can't now recall. I think he was a captain in the reserve force, so I might be able to recall his name if I really put in a lot of effort but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were in Kosovo in 1999, did you see any volunteer units in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, it says here 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I meant 1999. Did you see any volunteer units in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, I was in Kosovo as a volunteer; but in the area of responsibility of my battalion, there were other volunteers. None of those volunteers ever, ever was able to operate outside the chain of command and the system of subordination that existed in the army; never, ever, it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in 1992 through 1995, when you were serving as a military policeman, did you see action in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you tell us that you left the JNA in 1995; and now going to paragraph 24 of your statement, you tell us you drove a truck and made trips to Kosovo six days a week.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I have to apologise. You said the JNA. Not the JNA. The Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're correct. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: And I didn't leave it. My contract expired and I went to another job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from 1995 to 1999, when you volunteered, you worked driving a truck to Kosovo six days a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of that job, did you become familiar with the main roads and bigger towns in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, I know Kosovo very well. I got to know it then. I know it still. All the major towns and also some of the smaller towns there, such as Orahovac, Lipljane, the villages around Prizren, Djakovica, Pristina, Kosovska Mitrovica. So I do know this area very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 57, you tell us about volunteering. When was that or how soon after the NATO bombing began was it when you joined up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: It says in my statement that when my brother was called up, that I volunteered. But in fact, I went to Kosovo before he was called up. I was in Kosovo on the 27th of March already, which means that I left my place of birth on the 25th. On the 26th, I went to the unit that sent volunteers down to Kosovo. It says -- actually, the towns are specified in the statement. Were you able to find it, or should I perhaps specify the towns? Can I do that in open session or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's in your statement in paragraph 20, 26, and 27.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: So on the 27th, I was already in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by what date were you actually in uniform and attached to your unit, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I put on the uniform on the 26th, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the commanding officer of your unit was a major who you've named in private session, and you've also mentioned a lieutenant. In your statement, you tell us that your 10- to 12-man unit was under him. What specifically was your unit? Did it have a name or a title? And maybe we need to mention that in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something while we're still in open session. If I may explain something to the Trial Chamber regarding your question about my arrival in Kosovo, or do you -- I don't know. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes. I do want, because it's very important. When we got to Kosovo, it was already night-time, in fact, we arrived in Djakovica. At the command post, there were quite a few buses with volunteer, and our battalion commander was there to receive us personally. Since he knew that only the volunteers were on those buses, no regular army, he said the following and I quote verbatim. Can you hear me? "Gentlemen, this is not Kosovo, this is not Bosnia, orders must be complied with. There will be no arbitrary actions. Those who engage in any such acts will be punished very severely." So we all took that very seriously. Now we come to your question. What was the criterion they used to pick the ten of us or so? But I think that on the basis of our service in the previous units they picked us. I think that was the criterion that they applied. So this is in answer to your question that you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you two things. One, you said when the battalion commander greeted you, he said: "Gentlemen, this is not Kosovo, not Bosnia." Did you mean --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. "This is not Croatia, this is not Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you understand that to mean by him saying that this was not Croatia and this was not Bosnia, and that orders must be complied with. Had it been different in Croatia and in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, an experienced officer such as my commander knew quite well that not all of us came to Kosovo with the same kind of intention, and that's why he warned us in this manner. Not all people came to Kosovo to defend it. There were some drug addicts there, for instance, who got there to steal things. There were all kinds of people. This man volunteers and you cannot prohibit him from going because you don't know who that person is, but then he warned us there would be no arbitrary acts and any attempts to do so would be punished severely. The chain of command was to be sacrosanct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, can we go into private session for a moment. I want to ask you a question about your particular unit and the men in it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could show the witness Exhibit P1323.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, I want to ask you about some insignia. This should come up on the computer screen in front of you. And I don't know if it's easy for you -- easy enough for you to see on the screen or if you would prefer to look at a hard copy, which I can have the usher hand you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I can see it. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of those insignia on the page; and if so, can you tell us by number which one you're talking about and to what group or unit it referred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I assume that the insignia marked as 1 is the insignia of the 63rd Paratroopers Brigade. Number -- second is the military police. The third is the standard Yugoslav Army insignia. 6 and 7 are the police insignia dating from any period, in fact, it's impossible to determine the period. But some of these insignia may have been worn in Kosovo, but I'm sure that 4, 3, that these were worn in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think you said before what number 4 was, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 2 I think you said also was military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, number 2 could be the military police. It could also be -- well, who knows. I can't really recall. From the 1990s until the year 2000 when the Army of Yugoslavia was established, the insignia changed practically every year. Many units wore different insignia, but they were in the same branch, in fact. So you had all kinds of stuff, but these are the typical insignia. Number three is the standard VJ patch, four was military police. I was in the military police, but I don't recall wearing the patch marked as 5. I don't know what period this dates from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1999, what patches did you have on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I think we had the Army of Yugoslavia patch marked as 3 and the number 4, and we wore it on a black beret or a black cap. This was the standard-issue uniform, if that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of the exhibit. I suddenly have the transcript up on my e-court page instead of the exhibit. I don't know if it's a technical difficulty or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us anything about numbers 8 through 13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, 8 and 9 I saw in the war in Croatia, but not in Kosovo; I'm sure of that. In fact, I didn't see any of these patches in Kosovo; I'm sure of that. I'm sure because in the area of responsibility of my battalion those patches were not worn. They were only the army patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about number 13?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I don't think that this one was present there, but I can't really see it. It's possible that it was worn, but who knows. Well, if it's a PJP sign, it probably was present there because PJP units were there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we now go to Exhibit 1324.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, next I want to show you a page or two with some weapons on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recognise those? Going from 1 to 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can. Number 4 is Hechler. Number 3 is a submachine-gun Skorpion, then we have the 82-millimetre mortar. And the one up there, that's cannon. I don't know the calibre. I wasn't in the artillery, so I can't determine the calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What weapon did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Number 1 on the image 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have as a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I had an automatic rifle, standard-issue automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to weapons number 3 and 4, do you know which units used those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I know about the Skorpions. They were used by tank units. That is their standard-issue weapon because they cannot carry rifles. Well, as for the Hechler, well, hm, it was people who acted as security officers for high-ranking officers who had them or state VIPs, if they would come in. I didn't see any such people, but -- well, perhaps these security people wore Hechlers or carried Hechlers. But usually in our country, people who had Hechlers were working in the field of security and then they would go out into the field and they carry Hechlers. As for the Skorpions, it's members of the tank units for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about items 1 through 5 on this page, if you recognise any of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Classical infantry weaponry. 5 is an M-84 machine-gun. Number 4 is a sniper rifle, semi-automatic; then this is a sub-machine-gun T-3. And these are automatic rifles with different kinds -- well, I cannot guess as far as their numbers are concerned, but at any rate this is classical infantry weaponry. There is nothing special here. It's standard-issue army weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was yours like any of these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 1325.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, next I'll show you some vehicles and ask if you can help us with these. How about numbers 1 to 4, do you recognise any of these and can you tell us who used them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, I can just guess. Number 1 is an APC. Number 4 is a Praga. As for the rest, well, these are vehicles that we did not use for the most part; my unit didn't. As for number 2, well, I can't see. It looks like a BVP, but it's not. No, actually, it looks like a BOV. It could be a BOV since it has these holes on the side; one, two, three, and then times 2, that would be six. It could be a BOV under number 2. Now, under number 3, who knows, maybe a kind of transporter; APC, 1 and 3; and then 4 would be a Praga, and 2 would be a BOV, combat armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about 5 through 8?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, 8 is a truck, TAM 110 classical military truck for the transportation of equipment and personnel. 7 is a Pinzgauer. Now, 6 can be a T-55 tank, and 5 can be 84. Now, maybe I made a mistake. It depends on which one is which. 5 is a bit lower, so that could be 84 -- well, you know what, I'm not very knowledgeable about tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anything you can tell us about 9 through 12?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I could tell you about 10. That is a BVP, combat vehicle of the police. As for the rest, I can guess, but it's pointless, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't want you to guess.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: We didn't use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any of these being used by any of the forces in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: 13, if I can see right, is a Puch. That's a vehicle in which officers travelled then and now. Nothing special. As for the other vehicles, I don't know. 15 is a Hummer, as far as I can see, and the other one is a Land Rover, as far as I can see, but we didn't have any such vehicles. We didn't have them and we didn't use them; as for the Puchs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I would like to show you Exhibit 1592 and ask you a question about that. Can you -- based on the uniforms and the insignia, can you tell us anything about what unit these two might belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours, the picture we see now shows soldiers who I assume had this picture taken for their own personal use. After all -- well, cross-bows. Cross-bows were not carried by members of units who were out in the field every day. Judging by the vehicle they have, it could be either a Pinzgauer or a Puch. Sirens, the bars they have, it could be a Puch, but the uniform is classical military uniform. Now, we cannot see what unit it is. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Exhibit 1596. This is the next one I want to show you, K90. Can you tell us anything about what unit or what force these men might belong to based on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, judging by what we can see here and judging by the appearance of these people and what they're wearing and their haircuts and their behaviour, well -- but in the background I see something that could be a reserve police unit. But I think -- well, it's pointless to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can't tell us anything about what unit they might belong to or what force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: They belong to the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I assume, because I don't think that an active-duty officer would allow himself to have men like these under his command. I mean, as for my own criteria regarding the military, this simply doesn't fit in. I mean, things like this -- what is written here on his sleeve? "Police." But the reserve policemen wore the same kind of uniforms like policemen, so it's debatable. But it's certainly not a regular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you next Exhibit P1599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move off that photograph, do you know the significance of the ribbons they're wearing? 070129.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For recognition purposes, Your Honour. When they go out on mission in order to distinguish themselves from other men, from other units, or from the enemy or God knows who. That's why they wore these ribbons, but not all of them all the time. The question is where this photograph was taken. I saw things like this in Bosnia, in Croatia, but I see that it says "police" on these uniforms. So let us clear this up. Policemen of Republika Srpska wore similar or almost identical uniforms like our policemen. So it is possible that this photograph was taken in Bosnia. It could easily happen that that was the case, because in Kosovo you could hardly find a forest [Realtime transcript read in error "force"] like this anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see reserve policemen in Kosovo during your time there in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, Your Honour, the witness said on the 28, 10, instead of force he said "forest." It's very hard to find a "forest" like this anywhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it said "force" in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It makes a big difference to the sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K90, one question about an earlier photograph, the one with the two men on the vehicle. We just saw the top of the vehicle. The net masks on the faces, were these standard uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, these photographs, or rather, the photographs that you spoke about just now was taken so that they could showoff to other people, their relatives, their friends, whatever. Because it was just made up so nicely, wasn't it? So it could not have been taken for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you answered my question about -- did you see reserve -- did you see reserve police in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I told you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you next Exhibit P1600. What can you tell us about these men? What force or what unit would they belong to based on the uniforms and insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I don't know. What a miserable unit. They also got all dressed up here so that they could showoff afterwards to the folks back home what big heroes they were and what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak in the microphone, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: K90, the interpreters are asking you to be sure to speak into the microphone when you answer. Can you comment on the uniforms and the insignia --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- what is this? Which force would these men belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I cannot say on the basis of the uniforms. See, if you were to look at their caps that is something completely -- well, I don't know. It's not identical, but I said a few moments ago what a miserable unit and the poor unit that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would they be army or army reserve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- well, you know what, let me tell you. When you say the "reserve army," "army reserve," if you think that this context of the army -- I mean, as for the unit I was in, there wasn't much of a difference between active-duty military and reservists. Orders were the same for all and the command was the same for all. It didn't matter whether someone was a reservists or an active soldier. He fully had to respect orders just like an active soldier, regardless of who he was. So if you thought that reservists in my unit -- well, they certainly could not have been like this, and to have their pictures taken like this. I mean, I'm not sure I can say -- they have different caps, so I cannot tell. I don't know what it is for sure. Well possibly -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Sorry. It is possible that this photograph was not taken in Kosovo either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that because have a look at the emblems.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at what the emblems say. Perhaps if we could read that, we could identify what this is all about; but this way, hardly, hardly. Now, if we look at the emblems that this man has, the one next to the vehicle, these are coats of arms and insignia that the KLA had. So on the basis of that, we can say that this was in Kosovo. But I cannot claim anything because the army did not have vehicles like these with a machine-gun mounted on them as far as I can see. It is certainly not an army vehicle. We did not have vehicles that had been altered this way. We had standard vehicles that had not been altered in any way; we, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who did have vehicles altered that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, on some vehicles that are not combat vehicles -- I'm not sure. I think they were Russian made. The police would mount machine-guns on them. Now, whether they did this at their own initiative or whether this was regular practice, I cannot say. But on some of their vehicles, there were machine-guns, like here, like on this vehicle. Now, I don't know -- well, the green -- I don't know. I shouldn't be guessing now. I cannot say whether they are policemen or soldiers. Well, it is not active-duty military, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question: Do you recognise the patch on their arms; the red-white-blue patch, for example, on the man on the front row left, do you recognise that insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I see that. This is why I put this question. If this could be enlarged, then perhaps I could identify who it is; but it is very small, isn't it? It is certainly not military insignia. The army had standard insignia, and we showed that under number 3 a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the patch and try to enlarge it for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you one more. I don't think I showed you Exhibit 1599. One other group of men and I want to ask you if you can tell us anything based on their appearance and their uniforms and insignia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: May I not comment on this photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me why you don't want to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, these people in this photograph that we see now, do they deserve to be commented upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand perhaps your feeling about that, but isn't the patch on the sleeve of that man on the chair on the far right of the photograph, isn't that the one you've identified as being the army patch, the army insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: It is an army patch, army insignia, but this is not the army. Poor would be the commander who would have such soldiers, if they were soldiers at all. The question is where they had this picture taken, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from your comments you would not consider this a group of professional army members because of their appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, sir. Your Honours, in the unit where I served as a professional soldier, even near that unit that I served in in Kosovo, the unit of the major whose name we are not going to mention now. Right. I mean, people like this -- like these did not have access to that unit and could not even be near that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you one more, and then I'll return to your statement to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit IC42.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: K90, next I want to show you some camouflage patterns and ask if you know what uniforms, what units, what forces these particular camouflage patterns might have been worn by in Kosovo in 1999. And if you could just go from upper left to upper right and then lower left to lower right and give us any comment you have on those patterns.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: The first one on the left, that is the uniform that was worn by policemen, but I think it was the reserve police force that wore this. I think this is one of the police uniforms. Up on the right-hand side, I think that this is the uniform that was worn by the PJP because I have a uniform like that at home, the top part and the trousers. I'm not sure, but I think that's it -- actually, I'm sure about that. As for the one down here on the left, I don't know whose uniform this is. I cannot guess because I do not see this clearly at all. And on the right-hand side is a classical military uniform. As for the uniform down here on the left, I'm not sure, I cannot say. And the other one on the right-hand side is classical military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Worn by the VJ in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Classical military uniform down here on the right, but not everybody. As many as we had -- well, most people had it. The dates varied, but they did have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to return to your statement; and in paragraphs 41 to 45, you talk about how your particular unit was involved in some villages telling the villagers to leave. You mentioned that Zub was the first village where you did this, and I think you said that was around mid-April. Do you remember the names of any of the other villages where you did this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, no. But there is this brook between Zub and the neighbouring village, so it's all on the same plain. Viewed from the border, there was this other village that was empty. I don't know when it was emptied. Probably the villagers left the village even before we came there, but those are the first villages near the border. Those are the villages that are closest to the border. Since our command post was in Zub in the house of an Albanian who was in his house; that is to say, the man had not moved out. When we withdrew, they withdrew together with us. In fact, we did not tell them to go anywhere, but they left with us. Not at any moment did we say to them that they should leave the state, the country. Now, what does that mean to relocate someone? If you take his documents away, if you throw him out, and if you tell him he can no longer come back to his house, that is expulsion. But if he leaves with you and then if he can go back to his own house and get his own stuff after a all, that is not expulsion. I don't know, perhaps the Judges can say what is what, but for me that is not expulsion. Why would they stay out there on their own at the mercy of aircraft? That is so illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 44 you say: "Each time we undertook this tasking ourselves." I wasn't clear on that. I read that. In English it could be understood to mean that you, your unit, on your own decided when and where to do this. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, no. I explained it to you on Friday. No. When I said "on their own," that is what I meant when I was speaking a few minutes ago; that is to say, that other soldiers did not take part, so that what I spoke of previously would not happen. That is to say, when we're talking about the Albanian people who do not like any kind of mingling with their families, that is it. That is to say, we respected their customs and we carried out their orders that were quite clear. I told you on Friday and I'm telling the honourable Judges now. I don't know how we would have reacted if somebody had protested and said they didn't want to leave. I don't know, perhaps the commander would have to come and tell them, but we didn't have any orders like that. If they didn't want to leave, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in connection with Zub that when you did this you told the villagers they had to leave within two hours. Was it a similar deadline in the other villages where you did this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, no -- well, two hours -- you know what? When there's a war going on, when there's a war going on, you always have to be mobile, so to speak. Since they had communication with the command, our command in Zub was in the house of an Albanian. Most of them knew that they would be relocated, so this is a deadline -- well, you know, together with us. They withdrew together with us. It wasn't that we had relocated and that they had stayed on or that they left and we stayed on. We left together with them; that is to say the army and the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this an appropriate time for the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we do that, Mr. Hannis. Could you look, please, K90, at paragraph 30 of the statement where you describe various members of your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these what you would consider to be professional soldiers representative of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I were to exclude the man who had this excess after the war and this one man who fled from Kosovo; as for rest I have no observations because they impeccably carried out the orders given by the commander. Never at any point in time were they tempted to engage an excess to work to the detriment of the country or after an Albanian, if that is what you meant just now. Never. There are men there with a past -- well, more or less perhaps they were just bragging. But anyway they carried out their orders impeccably over there, and I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have to break at this stage, and we'll be out of court for about 20 minutes or so. We'll go into closed session while arrangements are made for you to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise. I can hear this terrible buzzing, this terrible buzzing in my ears. Yes, now it's much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that was the sound of the blinds going up, and it should be stopped now. Can you hear all right now? Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I went on, I wanted to follow up on the question that Judge Bonomy asked you just before the break. He asked you a question about the men in your unit, and you said with the exception of two; one who fled, and I gather from paragraph 30 of your statement that's the one you describe as getting into his car one day and never returning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the other one you referred to is one who was involved in excess after the war, and I take it by that you mean the one who is currently in prison for murdering a taxi-driver and his father in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I was talking about your unit going around in some of the villages and asking the villagers to leave. Did you speak to them in Serbian -- well, first of all, do you speak any Albanian yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then did you tell them in Serbian that they had to get out within two hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Your Honours, those were not orders. Those were not orders. This was -- I cannot really explain this. I can try. In fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just concentrate on the question. What language did you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation. Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you tell them where they were supposed to go when they left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That they should go towards Djakovica, the villages that were closer to the town, and the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the villagers that you had told to leave and go towards Djakovica, did you or your unit later take any of them back to their original villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Not until the end of the war, but they would come back to get the stuff that they needed from their homes. They were allowed to go there if they needed anything, flour. Whatever they had in their homes, they were allowed to go there and fetch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that, in paragraph 40 -- yes, 45, you say: "After we had ordered a village to leave, within an hour it was like an atom bomb had hit the village. Soldiers were coming through the village and looting everything that was not nailed down." Which soldiers were these? From where did they come, the ones who were doing the looting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Now, what I told you on Friday - and I will repeat now in front of this honourable Trial Chamber - no one could carry anything with them. But it happened sometimes that an individual would come by. If it had been a group, we would have seen them and they would have ended up in prison. But individuals would go in and search for things that they needed, but I think that some people that did that were actually drug addicts. They were trying to find things that they needed. And I can guarantee that nobody could or was allowed to take anything with them throughout the war in Kosovo. In my unit, I don't know about the other units, but in the unit where I served, nobody was allowed to touch anything that belonged to somebody else. People that were caught doing that were prosecuted and ended up in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In that paragraph, you go on to say: "They were taking things that they could not imagine they were going to be able to take home to Serbia." What kind of things were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to tell you. When I say that it looked as if an atomic bomb had exploded, they didn't take anything with them. They just rummaged through the stuff. They would cut into things looking for the things they needed. I don't know if you see my point. They were looking for the stuff that they needed because they were not able to take anything with them, yet they were rummaging through stuff, turning it upside down. They were looking for stuff, but these were not groups of people. They were individuals that we could not see. Had we been able to see them, they would have gotten what they deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that translation reads as though they were taking things -- I read that to mean they were taking big things like TVs, refrigerators, things they couldn't carry. Isn't that what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Do you think that we would not have seen them, that they wouldn't be seen? We cleared up this looting issue, the circumstances in which it took place. And when the time comes, we will explain this to the Trial Chamber. But if we're talking about this specific event, these events, these were individual incidents that you could only do something about it if you happened to come across this person doing that, and then you were -- would be able to arrest that person. We learned about most of those incidents from the people whose houses had been looted in this way, and I have to tell you it was not nice to sit there and listen to those stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say in that paragraph: "There's a lot more that I could say about the looting that went on." Can you tell the Judges what you meant by that. What's the "lot more" that you could tell us about the looting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I'm referring here to what happened on the last day, the last day. If you want me to, I can explain to the Judges about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. By "the last day," you mean when the war ended and the VJ forces withdrew from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: At the end when the forces pulled out, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Since our brigade had during the war about 13, 13 and -- 13.000 people, maybe 13 and a half approximately, and our battalion - the battalion has about 500 people, that would be the normal strength - but we had 3.000, 2.500 people and there were -- there was a certain number of officers commanding the 500 people. And I assume that with the influx of a greater number of soldiers during the war that there were more officers. If we multiply the number of officers even by 10, we cannot have more than a hundred officers there. On the day of the pull-out, the reservists were mobilised together with their vehicles. No officer -- not because they didn't want to, they couldn't physically do that. They were unable to check what people were taking with them. There was not enough fuel. A huge number of people had to be evacuated. You had to make sure that people didn't do anything inappropriate, and it is impossible to secure this huge mass of people. You could not control whether anyone was looting. There was looting. And on that day, the last day, there was looting because it was impossible to physically check each and every vehicle. They were driving their own vehicles, and we even had some rather unpleasant circumstances and incidents when we got to Serbia. Those people at one point simply fled to their own homes. You could shoot this person and he is adamant. He wants to go home. He wants to go home, this is my car, and he wants to go home. They would just get together, a couple from the same village, the would get on a truck, and they would just leave. It was impossible, physically, to control this whole thing. So this is what happened on the last day. Physically, it was impossible to control these people, to check what they were doing. If we had had our military vehicles, sufficient for the number of people that we actually had, we perhaps have been able to do that. We didn't have enough fuel. We didn't have enough vehicles. You have to drive the people; that was our priorities. So, in fact, you had acquiesce to what was going. It was impossible to control it. It was impossible to prevent these people from doing what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about that. I think it's on page 41, line 22. You say,"On the day of the pull-out, the reservists were mobilised together with their vehicles." Is this a group of reservists who had not yet been mobilised for the conflict, who were mobilised the last day before the war ended to come to Kosovo and help with the pull-out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, no. Sir, Your Honours, when a person has his privately owned truck, when he goes to register the truck, this truck can get its wartime assignment, be part of the reserve, just as a person. And these people would come in with their own vehicles. Sometimes your vehicle would be mobilised; and you, yourself, its owner would not be mobilised. So, for instance, your truck is mobilised and it takes part in the war, but you yourself don't. So it -- you don't have to drive your vehicle. At the beginning of the war, that's how people came in. They did not come on the last day. They were already there, in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So these were vehicles and reservists who had previously been mobilised, and they used their private, mobilised vehicles to help with the departure from Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No. They were already in Kosovo. There has been a misunderstanding. The vehicles and these people were already there when the war broke out. When the mobilisation was declared, they had to report to the unit where they were assigned. So in simplest terms, that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand now. In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your leaving --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm about to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're leaving this paragraph. Does that mean the witness hasn't said anything about looting at the time people were ordered to leave their villagers?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood him to say that they heard about it from the villagers, and he was aware that individual soldiers were involved in looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K90, in your statement, which you signed, your initials are on every page and your signature is on the statement, you say that after you had ordered a village to leave, soldiers were coming through the village and looting anything that was not nailed down. Now, you signed that as your statement. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, Your Honours, the way it is written in the statement, one would assume that this was general practice, that the troops would move through and loot everything. The point is these were individuals that were not under anyone's control. So this was not the general practice in the army. You said that I did sign my statement. There had been some mistakes in the translation, even in the parts of the statement that precede this. I don't know if you get my point; if not, I will try to clarify this some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly don't get your point, and I am going to seek for more clarification. Mr. Hannis, when this statement was signed, what language was it in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, he signed the English. This was the practice at the time, that it was composed in English and then it was read back to him. At page 12 of the statement, you'll see the interpreter's certification, that she orally translated the above statement from English to Serbian in his presence, who appeared to have heard and understand. And he acknowledged the facts and matters set out as translated by her were true to the best of his knowledge and recollection and signed it and initialed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your statement, K90, gives the impression that as soon as people left their village, the army were through that village taking everything they could lay their hands on from the houses there. It's as clear as day that that's what your statement says. Why did you sign a statement to that effect when you're now trying to claim that that was not the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not quite sure whether this was read back to me. I did sign the statement, but I claim -- where would they take the stuff with them if they -- if they really had taken the stuff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a very --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite illogical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the very point you make in the statement, that it was illogical. It was just done for the sake of looting. It wasn't done to obtain property; it was done to cause damage in the area, the very point you make in your statement. And now you seem to want to change that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I said is that individuals caused damage; that's true and this is not something that I'm contesting now. But this was not army in general. If you say,"the army," that would imply that there was a huge group of people moving through and looting stuff. But there were individuals doing that and this is not something I'm contesting at this point. Because there were errors in translation from Serbian into English in the statement that I was shown when I got here. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But you have not chosen to change that in the statement prior to coming in here today. So we can assume that you've checked this over and that seemed to you to be accurate when you checked it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did clear this up with the Prosecutor. I told him on Friday, literally, that those were individuals not a large group of people, if we don't take into account the last day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I also wish to draw your attention to paragraph 30 of your written statement where you mention about the composition of the units, and you talked of the variety of people that got into that and the characteristics of people and how they abandoned and how they ran away. But later when photographs were shown to you, you were being hysterical about the faces and about those persons, and you are showing a surprise, as if those persons who were in the photographs shown to you today were persons who could not belong to a unit. Now, how would you reconcile these things, please? And you, I think, parried the question whether they were of the army, despite an insignia was shown to you. How do you reconcile with this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the people you saw in the photographs are not people from my unit; that's the first thing. The second point, as for your question, apart from the man mentioned in the last paragraph of -- last part of paragraph 30,(redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), the rest of them acted quite properly. And the people that you mentioned, the people in the photograph, are not people from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. He mentioned a particular name, Your Honour, that maybe we should redact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. We shall. Witness, the -- you referred to Russians also. What uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same as we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You referred to somebody with long hair. You referred to a murderer. You referred to a deserter. Now, this is a unit you were proud of, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the man with the long hair was not a criminal, at least he did not exhibit any signs of criminal behaviour there. As for this other man, if he was tried, he could have said anything. We didn't have any evidence; but while he was there, he was behaving completely properly at all times except on one occasion. He didn't cause any problems because, otherwise, he would not have been there. So he had to abide by the rules very strictly. After all, the man with the long hair -- I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness K90, we, as a Bench, are not entirely satisfied that you are doing your best to comply with the solemn undertaking you gave at the beginning to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And we warn you now to be very careful about the way in which you're giving evidence to this Trial Chamber. Please reflect carefully on that, and make sure that throughout the rest of your evidence you comply with the undertaking to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move now to paragraph 46. Witness K90, you mentioned two occasions where there were NATO bombing that involved civilians on the ground. We talked about one before. I want to ask you about Djakovica. Do you know the circumstances of that one? We've heard evidence about bombing of a convoy near the Bistrazin bridge outside Djakovica. Is that the one you're referring to in your statement, or are you referring to a different one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I did have this incident in mind. On that day, I was in Prizren; and on our way back, there were some civilians and there were columns heading in all directions. Some people were going in one way and some people were going in another way. There were troops along the road, I mean military vehicles at that time. Now, I told you that I had heard that there was a military vehicle near the column when the air-strikes had taken place. I think this is what I wrote in -- this is what it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- who did you hear that from, that there had been a military vehicle near the convoy at the time of the strike?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I heard from the soldiers. I didn't have any official conversation with any person about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move now to paragraph 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where does that -- or how does that(redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have to make a redaction there, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That refers to another incident. He talks about two. The one you've just mentioned is the one involving Korisa, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your question -- I'm sorry. I assumed that that was also the incident involving the Bistrazin bridge, but, sorry, that's at Djakovica, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Bistrazin is a short distance outside of Djakovica I think to the south-east. We had another protected witness, I think it was K72, who testified about that incident as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to move to paragraph 47 of your statement, Witness K90, and you talk about there had been a killing of five policemen in an ambush in April; and after that, there was a mass deployment of police in the area. You talked about an additional 400 police who arrived in the Djakovica area, and among these were PJP and Frenki's. Can you tell us who the Frenki's were and what kind of uniforms and hats they wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, since one of the men in my unit used to be a reserve -- a member of the reserve of that unit, I heard from him that this unit had arrived because they wanted him to re-join the unit. As for the other policemen, they were brought in by bus, a number of buses, maybe about ten buses. Some drove their own private vehicles from all over the place, but that was on the day when the incident took place. They didn't arrive before, but on the day of the incident, and it says here that they arrived on the day when the incident occurred. So they didn't come the day before, but on the day when the incident occurred; and in the light of the fact that there had been some people in the town already --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: -- there were some police officers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, the question was: "Could you tell us who the Frenki's were and what kind of uniforms and hats they wore?" Now, could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume that if you're referring to Mr. Simatovic, that would be the unit for special operations. They wore red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Let me try and remember. No, I can't remember. I really have to apologise. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about paragraph 48. This is -- you talk about your unit was ordered to surround and secure the area around Korenica and Meja. When you say "your unit," do you mean just your unit of ten or 12 men, or do you mean your entire battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I told you already. This was not surrounding. We were tasked with blocking a section of the road that I actually drew on a diagram. Between the village and Djakovica, there was a stream there. So it was not the whole battalion, just part of the unit. Some people had come in from the border-posts, some people had already been there, maybe 100, 150 troops, our troops. Now, in the other areas, the other side of the village, and any other places, I didn't go there and that's what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say: "Once the area was secured that a large number of police were deployed, and they entered villages and randomly fired into homes." Do you know where these police were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No. I don't know where they had come from, but these were the police that arrived on that day on the buses. They went from house to house in the village, and it is correct that they did fire shots on the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any resistance coming from the villages as this was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any, because I was not in a position to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P326.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, I want to show you an exhibit that was used with another witness that shows the area. It has some markings on it. I want to ask you what your knowledge is about where you were located at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we can enlarge it a little bit for the lower half of that exhibit, and once more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to recognise the area that's depicted on here? We see the town of Djakovica in the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see where the villages of Meja and Korenica are listed on there? It's -- Korenica is partially obscured by one of the lines drawn, but do you recognise that area as depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: These are the villages near Djakovica. Well, I see the village of Meja, and I see where this line is for the village of Korenica. So it's the road to Junik. That is where part of my battalion was deployed, on the road itself and in part of the brook leading to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you also see the village of Brekovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Brekovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a crossroads in connection with your evidence. Is that crossroads depicted on this map, or were you talking about some smaller road that doesn't appear here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I cannot see the road forking off from the main road to Junik, going uphill on the right to a hamlet, a hamlet of the village of Korenica.
