That road cannot be seen, but -- just a moment, please. I think that that little road, yet another little road that leads to Meja near the river, you can't see that either. Well, maybe one can see it, but then I just cannot see it. There is the river and then next to the river there is a village and a mill and these big houses lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you be able to indicate on this map approximately where you were located, or is it too hard to see? Because if you can, we have a pen that you can use to mark on that map with, but let me know whether you think you're able to do it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you can just put a number 1 and draw a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: If this is the village of Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you've drawn a circle at the bottom of the arrow under the heading "check-points."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: The check-point was here at the bridge between Brekovac and Djakovica; here, right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you've drawn a circle on the red arrow that goes into the south-west corner of Djakovica to indicate the check-point. Now, based on that can you give us an approximate location of where you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Village of Brekovac, if I can see right. Between the village of Brekovac and Djakovica, that's where the check-point was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we give that an IC number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before we do, can you help me, Mr. Hannis, to understand how this ties in with the reference to securing the area around the villages of Korenica and Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think when he gave his answer to that he said -- he indicated that his particular unit was involved in setting up blockade related to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, witness? Were you securing the area or blockading one exit from the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, it's just a road. One side of the road towards Junik, and part of the brook that goes uphill. On this map you cannot see that part. On the left-hand side, it is the hamlet of Brekovac and on the right-hand side is the hill and then the town of Djakovica, or rather, the neighbourhood of Cabrat; that's the way it is supposed to be. This is what I can visualise right now, even from this distance, where things were. On this map -- well, that road is not there going next to the hamlet of -- well, not Brekovac, Korenica. So that's how I could show you where the brook is because there's this little valley there, too. If you can find it on the map somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This started off, Mr. Hannis, with a reference to a crossroads in the evidence. Now, where is the reference to the crossroads?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reference to the crossroads is in paragraph -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I've lost it. Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it 50 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 54 makes one reference to it and paragraph 51 makes a reference to it regarding the location of his command post vis-a-vis the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I explain. Perhaps it's going to be easier for you to understand if I explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, where is the diagram?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- it's attached to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, the question doesn't give me the information that I need to try to focus on what the issue is here. It's a bit disjointed, if I may say so, the way in which this is being presented. And if we look at this diagram, do we not get a clearer idea of the areas we're talking about? Why are we using something different when he's prepared his own diagram?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was trying to use this map because it -- it shows a broader area that is pertinent to something that I want to argue from about his evidence. And perhaps the map in the Kosovo atlas, Exhibit P615, at page 22, which shows Djakovica, Meja, and Brekovac, may be helpful to us if we can bring that up for the witness. Unfortunately, the page break in the Kosovo atlas leaves Korenica on the preceding page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, have we done a screen shot of what's there now? If not, I'd like to have that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's do that first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've moved away from blockades such that it might be of Korenica, is that right, and we're on to another subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to show him a map -- a another map and see if he can indicate on that map where he was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this would be Exhibit P615, the Kosovo atlas. I see that it's on the screen. Now -- I'm sorry, we need page 22. Yes. And if we can zoom in on Korenica, and the south-west side of -- south-west side of Djakovica, I'm sorry. And enlarge that. The square with Djakovica in it would be the best centring point. And one more, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you see that now? It shows Brekovac and Meja and the river and Djakovica. Are you able to orientate yourself on that map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me see. I see where Djakovica is. I see where Brekovac is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see Meja above that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I see Meja. That road -- well, there's this road here towards Korenica, and that area - it's an asphalt road - and that's where the crossroads is that causes confusion. So there is this dirt road going to the village, it's not an asphalt road, and that's why it is causing this confusion. That's the crossroads, and it's not marked on this map. And Meja is not on the same road, sir. Meja is by the river, and Korenica is on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we then show you your diagram, which is a part of your statement, and I believe it's page --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- page 18. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I don't see a picture here. Oh, the sketch that I drew?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, it's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It's in Exhibit 2391, page 18. Do you have a copy of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I hand the witness a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while we're trying to get that up on e-court, what is that a diagram of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: On this diagram, we see the road leading towards the village of Korenica and through Korenica. That is this main line in the middle. The line on the left of the diagram where it says the village of Meja, Selo Meja, that is also a road, that is not an asphalt road, that is behind the bridge for the village of Meja; and then there is this arrow where it says

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That is the road that causes confusion. That is a dirt road, not an asphalt road, that goes uphill to one of the hamlets of the village of Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that the crossroads you're referring to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your command post was located where on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Where it says VJ, 80 to 100 metres. As I said here, that is roughly the distance to the crossroads, between the crossroads and us, that is. So it is in that area somewhere. Soldiers who were in the blockade, our blockade, were -- can I somehow show you this on the diagram where they were? Somehow, can I circle it or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You can use the pen to mark on the screen, if you'll explain to us what you're doing as you do it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I'm marking the place where the blockade was, from here to somewhere around here before you enter the village. And here there is this small, very small village road leading also to the village of Meja. Over here there's a brook, here in this area, here. And that is where there were perhaps ten or 15 men in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me slow you down because it's hard to follow. First of all, you drew two lines to show where the blockade was. Can you draw a line connecting those two small lines to show the area of the blockade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've drawn a line connecting those, which seems to run parallel to the road toward Korenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: To the road, the left side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of the blockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, that if, as they have put it, if possibly members of the KLA were to come from the forest here, the forest is right here, through these fields, if they crossed the river, and if they moved towards Albania, that we possibly stop them in that situation. That's where the forest is, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've indicated with a series of dots and dashes on the upper right-hand portion of the drawing the area that you say is where the forest is located. Now, you started to draw a line at the top of the blockade area to the left you indicate -- is that a dirt road leading to Meja? Is that what that line is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, it's not a -- well, perhaps you can drive a car along part of it, but it's more of a footpath. It's a footpath through a field. I don't think a car can get through; but perhaps in part of it, say from these houses here, here, in this area, perhaps you could take a car here, but not in this area out here, not in this area here. But there is where people can get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this I think is putting Meja in a different place from where it appears in the Kosovo atlas, and it may be that an earlier witness identified this as a problem. I certainly have something in mind about the atlas being said to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe I recall that as well, Your Honour. There was some discussion about which side of a particular location Meja was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, on this diagram, can you tell us which direction would be north, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No. But I know for sure that the village of Meja, the houses of the village of Meja, are right on the river here, on the river itself. There's the mill here and then part of the hamlet and then the second part and the third part, and that's how the houses in Meja go. But I think this is Korenica, this, and there's no doubt about that. That's what we thought. And the first houses I marked are the village of Meja. At least that's the way I knew it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Meja is marked on your diagram in the upper left-hand corner with a series of small boxes; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say the river ran through that -- through that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, next to it, on the left side of the village. The village is on the right-hand side and the river is on the left side, behind the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the line you've drawn from the top of the page alongside these houses that you've marked as Meja, does that represent a road or a river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honour. Well, possibly -- well, it can be the road, but then the river also runs along the parallel line. Look at the bridge. I drew it here, and the village is -- and the river is right behind the village here, through Meja and Brekovac, between them; and then the graveyard is somewhere around here and then the village continues on the other side, Brekovac up to Deva and the Deva mine. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You've just drawn a red line that runs roughly parallel to the road from Meja to the first most or bridge, as you've marked it on your diagram. That represents the river. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: The river.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a little square you drew to the left of the river below Meja, is that the cemetery I think you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Cemetery, yes, graveyard, in the village of Brekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this diagram at the bottom, there's another most, or bridge, I take it. Is the line between the two most, is that a river or is that a road or does it represent both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: A road, a road, a road, just a road. As for the river, it's somewhere around here, and there's this curve -- well, I didn't go on that side, so I don't know. But I think it moves on from here further on, because I know that there is this curve; and then on the other side, there is a bridge again, on this side. So -- well, roughly, it's that part. I know that because there is this hill here. Now, this is the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've drawn a slight ellipse in the lower right-hand corner to represent a hill, and before that you drew a continuation of the river between the first bridge and the second bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, roughly, that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before we leave this one, let me ask you two questions. The crossroads where you saw the policemen taking men out of the line of villagers leaving the area, is that on this map; and if so, could you put an X where it's located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: It can be seen on the map. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us from which direction were the Albanian civilians coming that you saw walking past your command post? You don't need to make a mark, if you can just describe in words for us where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: They were coming from the area where it says "Korenica" towards this crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we give this the next IC number and take a screen shot, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what Mr. Hannis wanted, but for us this is totally unclear, unusable. And I suggest that we show him part of the transcript tomorrow and that then he shows us on the map what part the witness was referring to. I mean, this does not have any numbers or any markings, and I don't think that it's going to lead us to a relevant conclusion for all of us. So I really don't know how to get out of this problem, but it is way to complicated and it does not correspond to what the transcript says. And after all, certain symbols are repeated several times for certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not the most elegant map I've ever had drawn, but I think in the end we were able to get sufficient description of what things were and where they were to be able to follow it from reading the transcript. I think the argument goes to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I agree with Mr. Visnjic's general comments about the confusion, but the basic points seem to be clear. The route from Korenica to the check-point is clear on the map. The location where this witness says Meja was is clear on the map. These are the most important elements for the presentation of the Prosecution case. The matter is open for cross-examination later, and, indeed, you can start afresh and have another one done, Mr. Visnjic. And, indeed, I'm happy, if you wish to invite the witness because I'm going to invite him to do something else as well overnight, but I'm happy to invite him to draw a further diagram for presentation in the course of your case when you come to cross-examine. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then I take it may be given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see the witness wanted to say something, and I'll ask him to do that once we have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, was there something else you wanted to say about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I may make a mistake in drawing these lines or perhaps I cannot say exactly where the river is or where exactly which hamlet is belonging to this village, but I cannot make a mistake in terms of the place where this event occurred and the direction in which people were moving. And I cannot make a mistake in terms of where the army was. I cannot make a mistake in terms of where my command post was, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are matters for us to deal with, not for you to comment on. Mr. Hannis will ask you the next question he wants to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, how long were you out at this location? Was it just several hours or more than a day? How long were you out there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: We came around 5.00 in the morning and returned -- well, it could have been 11.00 or 12.00. After that, a few days later, we went to the same area again and then I went yet another time, the following day, I came to that area. So in fact, it was three times. And once when we went to Junik, it could have been, say, about 15 days later, we took the same road again. So that was probably the fourth time that I was there in that area; however, I have to say that from the river on, there is this flat land. I went to the Deva border post several times. That can be seen on -- well, the site, the place where this occurred, and the road can be seen. So I could not have made a mistake about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, though. Which of these occasions that you were out there was the one where you saw the civilians taken out and taken to a house and shot? Was it the first? Second? Third occasion? Which time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, the shooting started -- well, in the village in front of us there was shooting all over, but then when the shooting started behind us, near the command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Which of the three or four occasions you told us you were at this location was it when the shooting happened? Was it the first day you were out there? The second time you were out there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: The first day. If I understood your question right, the first day when the blockade took place. That was roughly the 27th. I'm not sure whether it was the 27th or the 28th of April. I cannot remember the exact date. I think that's when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, was this the day -- you tell us in your statement about one of your unit, one of the men in your unit being --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- shot and wounded. Was that the day that this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how long did you see civilians coming down the road by your command post during that day? Was it the entire time you were out there or only for an hour or two or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Almost all the time. The last group that I referred to in my statement came when the commander had already gone to the hospital to see what had happened with those men. So the blockade was already over. So it was practically a constant thing, that they were coming, that is; group by group, group after group, and that's the way it was, sometimes more, sometimes less. But the last group was between eight and ten men, and they came only after the commander had gone to the hospital, or to put it more correctly -- well, no. The hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 54, you mention about a group of about 30 policemen at the crossroads. And I think you told us before these were the policemen who had arrived before. These were the PJP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I think -- in fact, I'm sure that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You describe how they were taking some men out from the civilian who were leaving that way. Did you see -- was -- could you discern any system or logic in how they were choosing the men to take out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Interestingly enough, I could not get the criterion they used to separate these people. I don't know why they did it. They did not put them to some test to verify whether such and such a person was a KLA fighter. I simply could not make any conclusions as to what was the basis for what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraphs 55 through 60 of your statement, you describe seeing how some of the separated men were taken away, you heard gun-fire, and you went over and saw bodies. And you tell us that your major told you to go see what was happening. What did you say to the policeman you contacted when you complied with your major's directive to find out what was going on? What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: That the major was asking what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did the policeman reply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: He was quite angry, and he said: "We're destroying the Siptars." Now, I clarified to you what this means. Let me clarify this to the Court. In fact, what he said was: "We're skinning the Siptars." That's what it means, and that's how it was translated into English. But it can mean something else. It can refer to something else, because this word "derati" does not really have to mean that you have your knife out and that you're actually killing this person with your knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, it was translated as "slaughtering Siptars." Do you want to correct that now and say it should read "skinning"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, on Friday we went over this. The interpreter explained to you what I meant when I said that this was his reply. The police officer could have said: "We're combing the Siptars," and that would mean that they were fixing their hair. Do you see what I mean? But what they meant was precisely what they were doing. They killed them, but they didn't really skin them. Do I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went back and told your commander about what you had seen, did he go and talk to the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if he called or radioed anybody or reported about it to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No. Radio equipment was not used very often because of the air-strikes, so no, not at that time; perhaps later or perhaps I just didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 62, you mention how one of the guys in your unit was wounded and that the major was angry because he thought that the police had done it. You say you knew there was no KLA in the area then. How did you know that, that there weren't any KLA in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, we knew because there was no fire from the Albanian side. So if you're clearing up a village, you're expelling these people, and you have no fire being opened at you, no police officers were wounded or killed, only the people in the blockade were killed. So it's quite logical. This means that there was nobody there to shoot at you; that's the only logical explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were any of you guys, any of you VJ guys, doing any shooting at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we've heard some testimony from other witnesses that the KLA typically used a different kind of weapon -- a different kind of ammunition that made a different sound than the firing from VJ and police weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that. The troops did not fire. No soldier fired. There would have been response if they had. As for the circumstances of the wounded -- wounding of this soldier, he didn't see where the round was fired. And the other two that were wounded were standing there at the crossroads between Meja and Korenica and that's where they were hit. (redacted) he was hit. I can't imagine -- it may have been a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll need to make a redaction there of a name, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's all right. I've done it before myself, Witness K90?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, just one second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's in line 3, page 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention two others being injured. Were these two other soldiers from the 549th Brigade that were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, from our battalion. They were stationed at the Deva border post. I have to apologise. Can I have a five-minute break, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is requesting a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're not so very far from our normal break, so what we'll do is break earlier than we would otherwise have done. So can we go into closed session quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some of the blinds have not been activated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, you mentioned one of your colleagues was shot on that day; and in paragraph 63, you say your major ordered you to travel with the ambulance and try and find out what had happened. You say on the way -- by the way, where did the ambulance take your wounded comrade? Where was the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: All three of them were taken to the outpatient unit in Djakovica and then to Pristina, with our ambulance to Djakovica and then they were taken to Pristina in I guess the ambulance that would -- that belonged either to that outpatient unit there or the hospital, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you go to Pristina or did you just go to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No. No, just to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there did you talk to the soldiers and try to find out how they had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: (redacted)I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll have to redact that name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't talk to the one man from your unit because he'd already gone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes. I went to get the other two so I spoke to them, and I spoke to some people who helped me get them into the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you learn based on those conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I learned that they had been wounded, that they assumed that they had been wounded by stray bullets fired by the police, that was their assumption, because there was nobody else to fire on them. They were there standing on the road between Meja and Korenica, the road that I indicated on the map a little while ago. There's a road there and they were standing there, and that's where they were hit. One of them was hit in the back, and one of them had a through-and-through wound in the thigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say, in paragraph 63, that on your way you saw some bodies on the side of the road near the entrance to Korenica, and at least one of them was a woman. How were these four bodies dressed? Were these soldiers? KLA? Civilians? What? Based on the clothes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, that was not on the road or on the route. You can see the houses drawn here right on this sketch here, that's the building here. I don't know if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're referring to your diagram, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the house here, that is why it was drawn in here. Those were civilians. They were not in uniform. I don't recall exactly what they had on. They were maybe 50 or 30 metres away from me, maybe even less, some 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see any injuries on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No, because I didn't approach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph, 64, you told us you came back and reported to your major. What did he say about the report or the suggestion that your men had been wounded by fire from the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Well, he was visibly angry, first of all, because of the events there at the crossroads and the wounding of our men. He was visibly upset. He was swearing, and that's when he ordered me to go there and to take the people who lived -- who were in that -- those villages up there by the river Meja and so on, to take them to Djakovica with another soldier. They were already ready, and I took them to Djakovica, as I described in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it just two of you, yourself and one other soldier, who escorted those villagers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you pick them up in the village of Meja that's shown on your diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes. They were on the road in the village. The whole column had already been set up. They had already been ready to go. There were no police, no army there. There were no police, no military there. But once these people there realised that there was shooting going on, they got ready to go. At first they didn't even know what was happening. When they saw that we did not have any bad intentions, they saw that there were just the two of us, that we couldn't harm them in any way. So when they saw that there were no bad intentions on our part, they followed us. We took them to the bridge at Djakovica, and then we let them enter the town; in fact, we didn't let them, but we asked the people there to let them through into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said before that you don't speak any Albanian. How did you and the other soldier communicate with these people, with these civilians? Did you speak Serbian and they understood you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: 95 percent of the Albanian men speak Serbian, perhaps even more than -- it could be that the younger generations don't; but those who were above the age of 25, they certainly do speak Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a conversation with any people in this group about who you were and what you were there for and what you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: We discussed all kinds of things. We had to rest because there was some old people there who couldn't walk that fast, so we had to take rest regularly along the route. But there was no mistreatment, no mention was made of that. We simply said something along the lines of: This really shouldn't be happening. Nothing official. It was the kind of conversation one would have with a person one knows very well, despite the fact we didn't actually know them. We didn't discuss the situation what was happening at the time, neither they nor us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there -- you mentioned there were old people in your group. Were there women and children as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about any --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- any military-aged men in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long a distance did you have to travel to go from the village to the bridge where you eventually took them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Almost two kilometres, maybe even more. Let me think a little bit. About two kilometres, perhaps a little bit more, perhaps a little bit less. You had to pass through the village of Brekovac, so it may be a little more than two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your diagram, it looks to me as though you did -- well, let me ask you. Did you have to go by or through the place where those 30 police you had seen earlier were calling out and killing some of the men, did you have to go through that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: On the sketch that you showed me, I drew in a small footpath here or a very small road here. There's another road here, but the main road from the village goes like this. We didn't take this road here. We went straight to Djakovica, so we didn't go past the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you got -- when you got to the, I guess, bridge outside Djakovica and turned the people over, who was at the bridge there? Was that police or was that VJ or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: We didn't hand over anyone to anyone. I took them as far as the bridge and there was a check-point there. The check-point was manned by the military police and some reserve police. In fact, there was an active-duty policeman and a couple of reservists -- reserve police officers. I don't know how many of them. They asked me: "Where are these people going?" (redacted) order that these people should go into Djakovica and that's how it was. There were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we'll have to make another redaction there of a name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you say you were driven back to the crossroad near your command post. Who took you back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I think it was a policeman. I'm not sure, but I think it was a policeman; and not just me, but also the soldier that was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you got back I think you say you saw another group of civilian men taken out and taken into the building and shot. How many men in that group?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: (redacted) He had already left the command post, and the blockade was already lifting; and then this group of people, eight to ten people, they were part of this larger group which was -- which I mentioned in paragraph 61. I said that there were eight to ten people, just men, only men, aged between 23, 24, and maybe 30. I don't know where they had come from. They passed by our command post and reached the crossroads. That's all I know. And we heard when they were ordered to sing songs, and they took them to the little house in the yard. From the place where we were to the house -- the little house, there is nothing impeding the line, nothing in the line of vision, nothing to prevent us from seeing them enter the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 66, you mention that the police burned the houses where the men had been shot during the day. Did you actually see them set those houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anybody else in that area, other than the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: At that place where that happened, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to your supplemental information. If I could have the usher hand you a copy. In paragraph 67, you say you knew about some other incidents that happened when you were in Kosovo. And on Friday you gave us additional information, and I think there -- under item number 8, items (a), (b), (c), and (d) about some other events that you knew about. I want to go into private session for a minute to ask you about one of them, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that to protect the security of the witness, or is it for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Both I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the other reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other reason relates to the identity of the two VJ soldiers he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any more questions for this witness. I do have some documents I wanted to tender in relation to his testimony; but because three of those documents have the name of an individual that we've been talking about in private session, I would like to tender those under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we do that, the supplemental information doesn't -- isn't an exhibit, so what is it you're expecting us to make of paragraph 8? You've asked some questions about (b), which are probably adequate because of what else you said to amount to some evidence. (C) is clearly something you would never be leading anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So (a) and (d) are not part of the case at the moment as I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're right. I either need to ask him about that or tender the supplemental information. I think in light of some of the discussions we had earlier, I would like to give that an exhibit number and tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we would be happy about that, Mr. Hannis. Either you're going ask questions about this or you're going to depart from it. So I think that's the choice that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. K90, I want to ask you about item number (d) in that supplemental information under number 8. It says: "Two civilians were murdered by two VJ soldiers outside Djakovica during the conflict." And you know that an officer named Mancic was prosecuted. You say here you know that he is no longer in prison. Do you know when he was released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I don't know when he was released. I did see him some 20 days ago, not more than that. So he's not in prison anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you think what his rank was at the time of the alleged crimes for which he was charged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: I think he was a major. I think that now he's a lieutenant-colonel, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions about that, Your Honour. I'll make some connection to that with regard to another document I want to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, in that regard, I propose to offer Exhibit 2567, 2568, and 2569. I would like to offer those and have those filed under seal. And if we need to go into private session to discuss their relevance and authenticity, I'm willing to do that right now if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last document, Your Honour, P962. This was a document that was brought in by General Delic; and while I have some reservations about some of those documents, in this case, this is a list of filed criminal reports against perpetrators in the 549th Motorised Brigade between May 1998 and July 1999. I bring to the Court's attention item number 103, which refers to Major Mancic as being prosecuted for war crimes against civilians and receiving a prison sentence of seven years, later changed to 14 years on the prosecution's appeal, to connect with this witness's evidence about what happened to Major Mancic; and part of our argument that we'll make about either lack of punishment or something less than full punishment. And there is one other entry that refers to some of this witness's evidence regarding Major Radic, that's item number 124 on the list. He was referred to in the witness's statement as being involved in theft, and this shows that he was prosecuted for Article 174, which appears to be vehicle theft, and released in 2003. So some corroboration on this witness's evidence, relates to our eventual argument about the degree and nature of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the item number relating to Mancic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I -- 103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any Defence counsel have any comment to make on this document? Very well, we'll admit these two parts; that's items 103 and 124. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You wish the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've still to decide what to do with the statement, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you now feel you've had an opportunity to clarify any matters in your statement that you felt weren't accurately represented in the written statement? Is there anything else that we haven't talked about that you feel needs to be explained or clarified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90
utterances.text: Let me just tell you, Your Honour, that it was not my intention to protect anyone who committed any crimes. Your Honour, at the time when we were in Kosovo, the people that you warned me about, they were acting in a proper manner, and that is why I was able to be satisfied with their conduct. I don't know what they did after the war or before their arrival in Kosovo. This is for some other authorities to determine, not myself. Other than that, I could agree with what you say; yeah, that's okay. Now -- I agree for the most part with the clarifications that we made today, that that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give us a moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness has a B/C/S version of the statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it it's a copy that hasn't been revised in accordance with the changes in the supplemental information?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it could be revised in accordance with these changes, could it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and we need to omit the paragraphs 3 to 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- that you indicated at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness K90, what we're going to ask you to do -- we'll be finishing shortly for the day. You have the afternoon free and, indeed, the evening. We wish you to read a version of the statement which will be given to you. Don't leave this building until you get it. That version will be updated with corrections according to what you've told us in the course of today and what you told Mr. Hannis on Friday. You should read it tonight and you should come back tomorrow with a note of any other alterations you maintain should be made to that statement, and we'll consider these in the morning when we resume. So do you understand what I'm asking you to do, to read your statement very carefully --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so you can tell us exactly if anything's wrong with it or, alternatively, whether you accept that it's all true. All right. So we'll deal with that again before we finish for the day in about 20 minutes or so. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan -- Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to request that we adjourn now. There's only five minutes left and it would not, I think, be productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we have 25 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, okay, whatever it is, Your Honour. Based upon the evidence that's gone so far, we've all visited and I think it would be very helpful to the Chamber if we had an evening to re-work what we intended to do because we may have a shorter and a much different approach to this witness. And we have no witness after this witness until Wednesday anyhow, and I can assure you that we'll all finish tomorrow without any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we are -- Mr. Hannis, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm seeking some guidance about the preparation of his statement. It's easy for me to put in the changes that were listed in the supplemental information. I know what they are. The changes he made during his testimony are less clear to me exactly what those should be. I guess I would like to see what he writes about those, and then prepare an amended statement to reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all I'm asking you to do is incorporate into the statement the changes which were clearly intimated in the supplemental information and the additional ones at the beginning of today's evidence which were clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Insofar as anything may have been qualified or supplemented in the course of oral evidence, I don't expect you to be revising the statement to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is an exercise that by -- that can be done very quickly as long as you have a B/C/S speaker available to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness will not leave here until he gets it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the statement that I and the Prosecutor prepared on Friday. I have my written objections on that statement -- well, it's not objections. It's things that were not translated properly. So that would be things that I don't want in the statement. So it's three minutes, really, not more than that. I just need to have this copied out on a different sheet of paper, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you will do, after going through the statement carefully tonight and making any additional notes you wish, is you will come in here and you will tell us directly, you will tell me directly the alterations that you wish to make to that statement. We're not going to do this in a rush just now. We're going to give you the time overnight to read it, and we rely on you to do that. And the Prosecutor will make sure that you've got a copy with only the alterations that have already been made by you clearly, and you'll need to start again and add any additional notes on to that so that you can tell us tomorrow what changes in addition you wish to make. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously, in doing that, you can use the copy you've already made notes on to make sure that you cover everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we're going to finish the proceedings for today, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. You have to be here ready to continue your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow. Meanwhile, you can have no discussion with anybody at all about any of your evidence, either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give in the case. So when you're doing the work we've asked you to do, you do it on your own. You have nobody to ask about that. You can talk to people about anything else, any other subject, but you can't talk to anybody at all - Prosecutor, Defence, anybody - about your evidence. Now, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you're dealing with this, you're entirely on your own. All right. Now we will go into closed session so that you can leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.29 p.m.,
